$$
∀n\in Z,\,6∣{n}^{2}+2.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀n\in Z,\,6∣{n}^{2}+2)\,≡\,∃n\in Z,\,6∤{n}^{2}+2
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $n$ such that 

$$
6∤{n}^{2}+2.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=0$ suffices:

Notice that by substituting $n=0$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}+2 & =(0)^{2}+2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

which is not divisible by $6.$ 

Finally, we state our conclusion:

$5n+2$ is odd for any $n\in Z.$

In other words, we need to show that {{field-3}}

Notice that by substituting $n=$ {{field-5}} into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5n+2 & =5({{field-6}})+2 \\  & ={{field-7}}\end{aligned}
$$

which is {{field-8}}. 

So, $n=$ {{field-9}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
∀n\in Z,\,5n+2\text{ is odd}.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀n\in Z,\,5n+2\text{ is odd})\,≡\,∃n\in Z,\,5n+2\text{ is even}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $n$ such that $5n+2$ is even.

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=0$ suffices:

Notice that by substituting $n=0$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5n+2 & =5(0)+2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

which is even. 

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $n=0$ is our counterexample. We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀x\in R,\,{x}^{2}+5x+6\ge 0)\,≡\,∃x\in R,\,{x}^{2}+5x+6<0

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists a real number $x$ such that 

$$

$$

By substituting $x=-2.5$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x+6 & =(-2.5)^{2}+5(-2.5)+6 \\  & =-0.25 \\  & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}5n+2 & =5(0)+2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

which is even.

So, $x=$ {{field-10}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$11n-{n}^{2}-28\le 0$ for any $n\in N.$

So, $n=$ {{field-10}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false." :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
∀n\in N,\,11n-{n}^{2}-28\le 0.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀n\in N,\,11n-{n}^{2}-28\le 0)\,≡\,∃n\in N,\,11n-{n}^{2}-28>0
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists a natural number $n$ such that 

$$
11n-{n}^{2}-28>0.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=5$ suffices:

By substituting $n=5$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}11n-{n}^{2}-28 & =11(5)-(5)^{2}-28 \\  & =2 \\  & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $n=5$ is our counterexample. ["question-7927d3cc-3f03-52c6-bf05-98c129843c5c" :question/math-academy-id "q-221701"] ["question-7927d3cc-3f03-52c6-bf05-98c129843c5c" :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

So, $n=$ {{field-9}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] ["question-7927d3cc-3f03-52c6-bf05-98c129843c5c" :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
∀n\in Z,\,5n+2\text{ is odd}.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀n\in Z,\,5n+2\text{ is odd})\,≡\,∃n\in Z,\,5n+2\text{ is even}
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $n$ such that $5n+2$ is even.

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=0$ suffices:

Notice that by substituting $n=0$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5n+2 & =5(0)+2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

which is even. 

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $n=0$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] ["question-7927d3cc-3f03-52c6-bf05-98c129843c5c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-03fc8aaa-3047-551e-96b6-c20a42fc7aa2" So, $x=$ {{field-10}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] ["question-fbf3d356-bb6f-5d45-9a65-7f6a6ff861ab" :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
∀x\in R,\,{x}^{2}+5x+6\ge 0.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀x\in R,\,{x}^{2}+5x+6\ge 0)\,≡\,∃x\in R,\,{x}^{2}+5x+6<0
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists a real number $x$ such that 

$$
{x}^{2}+5x+6<0.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $x=-2.5$ suffices:

By substituting $x=-2.5$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x+6 & =(-2.5)^{2}+5(-2.5)+6 \\  & =-0.25 \\  & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $x=-2.5$ is our counterexample. So, $n=$ {{field-10}} is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."] ["question-65f2c34a-43ea-5ba9-8212-652326193c1e" :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
∀n\in N,\,11n-{n}^{2}-28\le 0.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
¬(∀n\in N,\,11n-{n}^{2}-28\le 0)\,≡\,∃n\in N,\,11n-{n}^{2}-28>0
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists a natural number $n$ such that 

$$
11n-{n}^{2}-28>0.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=5$ suffices:

By substituting $n=5$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}11n-{n}^{2}-28 & =11(5)-(5)^{2}-28 \\  & =2 \\  & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

${n}^{2}-6n+8\ge 0$ for any $n\in N.$" :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
∀n\in Z,\,{n}^{2}-6n+8\ge 0.
$$

Since this statement is false, its negation is true. 

A *counterexample* is a particular case that disproves the statement. Equivalently, it's a case that proves the negation is true. 

The negation of our statement is

$$
¬(∀n\in Z,\,{n}^{2}-6n+8\ge 0)\,≡\,∃n\in Z,\,{n}^{2}-6n+8<0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

A counterexample for the above statement would be an integer $n$ such that 

$$
{n}^{2}-6n+8<0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409537 :question/id #uuid "e3db273a-c488-5a82-8422-fe1e9221beaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-221691" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186171929 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

Since this statement is false, its negation is true. 

A *counterexample* is a particular case that disproves the statement. Equivalently, it's a case that proves the negation is true.

$$
¬(∀n\in Z,\,9n-4\text{ is even})\,≡\,∃n\in Z,\,9n-4\text{ is odd}.
$$

$2 \mid n^2-3$ for any $n \in \mathbb{Z}.$" :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \mid n^2-3.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\neg \big( \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \mid n^2-3\big) \: \equiv \: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \not\mid n^2-3
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $n$ such that 

$$
2 \not\mid n^2-3.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=0$ suffices:

Notice that by substituting $n=0$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-3 & =(0)^{2}-3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

which is not divisible by $2.$ 

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $n=0$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."} {:db/id 17592186172420 :question/id #uuid "e4478255-75d0-5395-b98c-a777a0ec14fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-184793"} {:db/id 17592186172422 :question/id #uuid "3a8ee06a-2fcd-5bc5-b6d4-f4628e18e15f" :question/math-academy-id "q-184824"} {:db/id 17592186171931 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171737 :question/id #uuid "331f2d85-cde0-5d83-abce-910d845845f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-13353"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "44e48ea1-2219-5954-8101-def7c9c2be2c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172419 :question/id #uuid "588d780c-a501-5839-b98d-b30c5c858804" :question/math-academy-id "q-184792"} {:db/id 17592186172453 :question/id #uuid "7079d3c8-051b-5896-b195-3be219a2a971" :question/math-academy-id "q-221837"}] :knowledge-point/title "Disproving Inequalities"} {:db/id 17592186171737 :question/id #uuid "331f2d85-cde0-5d83-abce-910d845845f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-13353" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186171931 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "44e48ea1-2219-5954-8101-def7c9c2be2c" :knowledge-point/title "Disproving Inequalities"}] :question/problem "Disprove the following statement:

$3q^2-2 \gt 0$ for any $q \in \mathbb{Q}.$" :question/worked-solution "Our statement can be written as

$$
\forall q \in \mathbb{Q}, \: 3q^2-2 \gt 0.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\neg \big( \forall q \in \mathbb{Q}, \: 3q^2-2 \gt 0 \big) \: \equiv \: \exists q \in \mathbb{Q}, \: 3q^2-2 \leq 0
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists a rational number $q$ such that 

$$
3q^2-2 \leq 0.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $q=0$ suffices:

By substituting $q=0$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{q}^{2}-2 & =3{(0)}^{2}-2 \\  & =-2 \\  & \le 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, $q=0$ is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false."} {:db/id 17592186172419 :question/id #uuid "588d780c-a501-5839-b98d-b30c5c858804" :question/math-academy-id "q-184792"} {:db/id 17592186172453 :question/id :topic/math-academy-id 3412} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186172710 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173297 :tutorial/content "To **disprove** a statement means to show that it is false. In this lesson, we will learn how to disprove universal statements.

Suppose we wish to disprove a universal statement of the form 

$$
\forall x \in U, \: P(x),
$$

where $U$ is some universal set. To do that, we must demonstrate that the statement's negation is true. 

The negation of this statement is

$$
\neg \big( \forall x \in U, \: P(x) \big) \: \equiv \: \exists x \in U, \: \lnot P(x).
$$

Therefore, to disprove a universal statement, finding one value of the variable that makes the negation true is sufficient. Suppose we wish to disprove a universal statement of the form 

$$
\forall x \in U, \: P(x),
$$

where $U$ is some universal set. To do that, we must demonstrate that the statement's negation is true. 

The negation of this statement is

$$
\neg \big( \forall x \in U, \: P(x) \big) \: \equiv \: \exists x \in U, \: \lnot P(x).
$$

Therefore, to disprove a universal statement, finding one value of the variable that makes the negation true is sufficient. This value is called a **counterexample** to the original statement." :tutorial/id #uuid "ac5efd40-5d78-5a92-a14d-9b292d2cf5dc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9356 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4b516377-68a8-5a1c-aae3-dfee168a79c0" :step/math-academy-id 162326 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172711}} {:db/id 17592186173297 :tutorial/content "To **disprove** a statement means to show that it is false. 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1008 "This course introduces students to proof-writing essentials, bridging the gap between pure problem-solving and constructing formal mathematical arguments. Students will formalize their understanding of logic, sets, and functions while delving into new concepts such as congruence, relations, and cardinality.
This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.
The prerequisite for Methods of Proof is single-variable calculus, which would be satisfied by completion of either Calculus II, AP Calculus BC, or Mathematical Foundations III." 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1009 "Students begin by mastering the basics of logic and logical operations, including statements, predicates, connectives, logical laws, logical equivalence, conditional and biconditional statements, quantifiers, inference, and formal and informal language. A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts

$2 \mid n^2-3$ for any $n \in \mathbb{Z}.$" 17592186045417] [17592186171733 1072 #uuid "753bc7ba-2d9a-598a-8b39-19d4292b6cdc" 17592186045417] [17592186171733 1074 "Our statement can be written as

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \mid n^2-3.
$$

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

$$
\neg \big( \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \mid n^2-3\big) \: \equiv \: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \not\mid n^2-3
$$

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer $n$ such that 

$$
2 \not\mid n^2-3.
$$

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting $n=0$ suffices:

Notice that by substituting $n=0$ into the expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}-3 & =(0)^{2}-3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$
